title: Crib Sheet
tagline: Turn your outline into an exam note sheet that fills exactly the number of pages your professor allows.
summary: Builds a dense Word file for exams where you can bring notes: landscape, narrow columns, cut to your page limit and filled to the bottom of the last column. It asks about your exam and how you like information laid out before it writes anything. For law classes it builds rule blocks; for calculation classes it builds step-by-step recipes.
whatItDoes: Ask about your exam first: class, format, page limit, paper size, open book or not, and how dense you want the text.
Build rule blocks for law: an attack order, then one table per doctrine with elements, "Here," analysis prompts, key cases in italics, defenses and traps.
Build recipe tables for calculation classes: given, numbered steps, a labeled shortcut, and a worked check with made-up numbers.
Fit the page limit by building, measuring and trimming until the last column is nearly full, then check the result by eye.
Mark key terms in yellow and add a green label to each element saying what it gives you, so you can find the right rule in seconds.
whenToUse: Use it when you can bring a note sheet to an exam and need your outline cut to a set number of pages, or when you want to shrink, refit or add to a sheet you already have. Check your course's AI and honor-code rules first: graded problem sets and take-home exams should not be fed to it.
examplePrompts: Make a crib sheet for my Torts final. One page, one side, covering negligence and strict liability.
Condense my Contracts outline into a 2-page attack sheet, 5 columns, case names only.
Here is my Evidence cheat sheet. It is 1.3 pages and the limit is 1. Cut it to fit.
Build a formula sheet for my Statistics midterm, weeks 1 to 6, with a worked check for each problem type.
whatChanged: Without the skill, Claude writes loose text with no control over length, so it runs past your page limit and you cut it by hand. With the skill, Claude builds the Word file, measures it against the limit, and trims until it fits, using a fixed layout where every element has its test, a "Here," prompt and its key cases.
